motion: Does scientific understanding leave rational grounds for belief in God?

routes.speaker: Francis Collins
routes.position: Scientific understanding leaves rational grounds for belief in God.

bridges.statement: Scientific findings do not prove God, but they remain consistent with and can contribute to a rational cumulative case for belief.
Evolutionary and other natural explanations can describe God's orderly means of creation rather than exclude divine purpose.
Lawful intelligibility, cosmic origins, and fine-tuning are evidential signposts that make a creator mind rationally defensible.
A stable law-governed creation can entail natural suffering while permitting rare, purposive miracles without contradiction.
Moral obligation, radical altruism, beauty, and transcendent experience add non-scientific but rational evidence to the cumulative case.

routes.speaker: Richard Dawkins
routes.position: Scientific understanding provides no need for God.

bridges.statement: Natural explanation removes the need to posit God and leaves belief without adequate explanatory support.
Darwinian evolution explains apparent biological design by a gradual bottom-up process from simplicity to complexity.
A creator mind is explanatorily costly and does not solve origins or fine-tuning unless its own complexity is explained.
Natural suffering and selective miracles sit uneasily with a loving God committed to stable natural law.
Morality, altruism, and beauty can be explained naturalistically without being demeaned or requiring divine grounding.

sections.title: lawful intelligibility, cosmic origins, and fine-tuning

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: that level of complexity needed a designer
when i finally understood the full magnitude of the darwinian explanation
no need for that
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley directly hands the question to Dawkins, whose first-person account continues throughout the span.
moves.proposition: Dawkins abandoned creator belief when he understood that Darwinian evolution could explain the biological complexity that had seemed to require design.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Dawkins's principal personal and scientific route to disbelief and frames his later no-need argument.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: questions that science wasn't helping me with
why is there something instead of nothing
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley explicitly hands the autobiographical question to Collins, and the first-person medical-school narrative is stable.
moves.proposition: Collins found that science did not address existential questions such as purpose, death, God, and why anything exists.
moves.inventoryRationale: The move supplies the epistemic premise for Collins's claim that scientific understanding does not exhaust rational inquiry.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: thought i would be able to shoot down all their arguments
faith was more rational than atheism for me
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person conversion account is clearly Collins's.
moves.proposition: After investigating theological arguments for two years, Collins judged his objections superficial and faith more rational than atheism.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is evidential biography rather than mere background because Collins presents inquiry and comparative reasoning as premises for rational belief.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: evolution is incredibly powerful as an explanatory science
i don't see how that in any way excludes the possibility
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley explicitly asks Collins to explain why evolution does not exclude God; this is Collins's uninterrupted answer.
moves.proposition: Evolution powerfully explains biological diversity, but that explanatory success does not itself exclude a divine plan; it moves the proposed plan to a deeper level.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Collins's core compatibility claim and an explicit concession to evolutionary science.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: wouldn't evolution have been a very elegant way to do so
outside of time
moves.attributionBasis: The same clearly attributed Collins turn continues.
moves.proposition: If a timeless God intended conscious creatures, evolution could be an elegant means whose outcome God knew without intervening in each step.
moves.inventoryRationale: This independently states Collins's positive model of providence through evolution rather than merely denying incompatibility.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: i would not use such a wasteful long drawn-out process
the very mechanism which actually makes him superfluous
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley asks Dawkins to respond to Collins while staying with evolution; the answer is clearly Dawkins's.

responseComponents.component: Challenges Collins's elegant-means proposal: an intentional creator would not need a wasteful process that can operate without the creator.

moves.proposition: Natural selection is an implausibly wasteful route for an intending creator and, because it can operate without God, makes God superfluous.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is a major direct objection to evolutionary creation, combining divine-method criticism with explanatory redundancy.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: natural selection is cruel
the suffering which comes from the fact that it's all about competition
it's not a benign process at all
moves.attributionBasis: The stable Dawkins turn continues until he explicitly minimizes this particular argument.
moves.proposition: Natural selection is non-benign: competition produces starvation, predation, disease, and extensive suffering.
moves.inventoryRationale: This introduces the biological suffering objection while preserving Dawkins's concession that he regards it as less important than his explanatory argument.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the fact that it took a long time should trouble us
outside of space and time it's a blink of an eye
moves.attributionBasis: After the break Brierley expressly returns Dawkins's objection to Collins, who answers directly.

responseComponents.component: Answers the long-duration objection by arguing that elapsed time is not a cost for a God outside time.

moves.proposition: Evolution's duration is not an objection from the perspective of a timeless God for whom the process is effectively instantaneous and its outcome known.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Collins's distinct reply to the temporal-waste component of Dawkins's criticism.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: god is really interested in order
follow these elegant mathematical laws
one of those signposts that i see of an intelligence
moves.attributionBasis: Collins continues his directly addressed reply to Dawkins.

responseComponents.component: Argues that an orderly law-governed process is fitting if God values natural order rather than instantaneous manufacture.
Places evolutionary costs within a wider law-governed creation rather than treating each outcome as separately designed.

moves.proposition: A creator interested in order could rationally choose evolution within elegant mathematical laws, whose intelligibility itself is a signpost of intelligence.
moves.inventoryRationale: The move joins Collins's evolutionary reply to his broader lawful-intelligibility case.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: does away with the need for any kind of top-down design
starts with simplicity and builds up to complexity
you don't actually need a designer
moves.attributionBasis: The dialogue switches clearly to Dawkins, who states his central Darwinian response at length.

responseComponents.component: Argues that Darwinism does more than remain compatible with atheism: it removes the explanatory need for design.
Rejects reintroducing intention behind a process whose achievement is explaining design from simplicity.
Denies that the law-governed evolutionary process needs top-down intelligence to account for complexity.

moves.proposition: Darwinism explains complexity and the appearance of design from simple beginnings, so adding top-down design betrays the explanatory achievement that made a designer unnecessary.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Dawkins's fullest central argument for bottom-up explanation against theistic evolution.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: starts with simplicity and builds up to complexity
to smuggle design in again at the beginning
is a betrayal of that whole argument
moves.attributionBasis: This is a clearly continuous portion of Dawkins's turn; it overlaps the thematic transition but states an independently assessable simplicity inference.

responseComponents.component: Contends that placing foreknown design at the beginning reverses the bottom-up explanatory direction.
Treats prior intelligence as an unnecessary reintroduction of the very complexity evolution explains.

moves.proposition: Because evolution builds complexity from simplicity, inserting design at the beginning reverses and undermines the bottom-up explanation.
moves.inventoryRationale: Although adjacent to m10, this isolates the distinct explanatory-direction argument that later grounds Dawkins's divine-complexity objection.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the evolutionary process is incapable of generating complexity i think it totally is
where did those come from
moves.attributionBasis: Collins explicitly addresses Dawkins by name and distinguishes their agreement from his next question.

responseComponents.component: Concedes completely that evolution can generate complexity, then redirects the dispute to the origin of the laws enabling it.
Argues that accepting bottom-up biological explanation leaves a deeper explanatory question about physical law.

moves.proposition: Collins fully accepts evolution's ability to generate complexity but argues that this leaves unanswered where the enabling laws of physics came from.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is an important concession and the pivotal transition from biological design to cosmic explanation.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if somebody was going to convince me of the need for a god
the origin of the physical constants
getting close to a good argument
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins responds immediately to Collins's question about the laws and explicitly contrasts physics with biology.

responseComponents.component: Concedes that the origin of physical constants is where a case for God would be strongest, unlike biological or moral arguments.

moves.proposition: Dawkins concedes that the origin of physical constants is the closest approach to a good argument for God, though he does not accept it as decisive.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is a major burden-relevant concession defining the strongest rational ground Dawkins recognizes.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if you change any of those constants by even a very very small amount
we don't come into existence
they have to be like that
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins continues uninterrupted, identifying constants and their life-permitting sensitivity.
moves.proposition: The physical constants appear highly sensitive: small changes would prevent galaxies, stars, chemistry, and the prerequisites for life.
moves.inventoryRationale: This records Dawkins's substantive concession to the fine-tuning datum rather than attributing the moderator's formulation to him.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we postulate a fine tuner
you haven't explained anything
something more complex to describe something already
moves.attributionBasis: After Brierley frames the issue, Dawkins's answer begins at event 943 and states the inference in his own words.

responseComponents.component: Answers the demand for an origin of laws by arguing that a fine-tuner merely relocates the unexplained complexity.

moves.proposition: Postulating a fine-tuner does not explain fine-tuning because it introduces something still more complex that itself requires explanation.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Dawkins's principal regress and explanatory-cost objection to cosmic design.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: fine-tuning is a puzzle that seems to ask for some kind of explanation
an infinite number of other universes
a bit of a leap of faith as well
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley hands Dawkins's objection to Collins, who begins with an explicit agreement and alternative explanation.
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning requires explanation; an infinite multiverse offers an anthropic alternative, but its apparent experimental inaccessibility also involves an evidential leap.
moves.inventoryRationale: This states Collins's comparison of the creator and multiverse hypotheses without treating fine-tuning as proof.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: god as being outside space and time
you've got an infinite regress problem
a much broader sense of what the existence of god would be like
moves.attributionBasis: Collins explicitly addresses Dawkins's regress argument in a continuous answer.

responseComponents.component: Rejects the regress objection by defining the proposed creator as outside space-time and therefore not subject to temporal beginning conditions.

moves.proposition: A creator outside space and time need not have a temporal beginning, so the demand for a creator of God does not generate the same regress.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Collins's direct answer to Dawkins's divine-complexity and regress objection.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: entirely rational and defensible as a position
it doesn't prove it of course
consistent
moves.attributionBasis: The answer follows a moderator clarification, but the selected span isolates Collins's own assessment and concession.
moves.proposition: Using God to explain why anything exists is rationally defensible and consistent with the evidence, though it is not a proof.
moves.inventoryRationale: This precisely states Collins's motion-level epistemic conclusion and preserves his explicit limitation.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the multiverse is something that comes from other aspects of physics
less convinced by the multiverse if it was just invented
a prediction of other reputable aspects of physics
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins explicitly qualifies his expertise while reporting the scientific basis he understands for multiverse proposals.

responseComponents.component: Answers the charge that the multiverse is an ad hoc leap by saying it is independently motivated by inflationary physics.

moves.proposition: The multiverse is less ad hoc than Collins suggests because it is reportedly predicted by independently reputable inflationary physics, not invented solely to solve fine-tuning.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Dawkins's main naturalistic alternative to cosmic design, with his uncertainty about physics preserved.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the ability to actually experimentally document the existence
extremely unlikely probably impossible
pick occam's razor here
moves.attributionBasis: Collins clearly resumes after acknowledging inflationary theory and directly compares the hypotheses.

responseComponents.component: Concedes inflationary motivation but argues that inaccessible universes remain experimentally untestable and therefore do not straightforwardly outrank a creator explanation.

moves.proposition: Because other universes may be impossible to detect, choosing between multiverse and creator explanations depends partly on prior probability rather than decisive experimental confirmation.
moves.inventoryRationale: This preserves Collins's measured comparative conclusion and acknowledgement that priors affect the inference.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: perhaps we both come at it
a bit of presupposition
possible to explain complex things in terms of simple things
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins answers Brierley's question directly and explicitly describes his own prior orientation.
moves.proposition: Dawkins acknowledges that both speakers approach the issue with presuppositions and that his is shaped by attraction to explaining complex things through simpler ones.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is an important epistemic concession concerning priors, paired with his substantive simplicity principle.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a big complex thing which god must be
throws a ruddy great spanner
the beauty of that darwinian concept
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted Dawkins turn continues and applies his simplicity orientation directly to God.
moves.proposition: A necessarily complex God disrupts the explanatory virtue of deriving complex outcomes through a simple gradual process.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is the compact positive form of Dawkins's complexity objection.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: god's got to be complex
god is totally simple
if he is simple he couldn't invent the fundamental constants
moves.attributionBasis: Although a brief moderator prompt occurs later, the selected span is Dawkins's continuous criticism of divine simplicity.
moves.proposition: Theological claims that God is simple are implausible because a being capable of choosing the fundamental constants would require corresponding complexity.
moves.inventoryRationale: This independently targets the divine-simplicity response to Dawkins's explanatory-cost objection.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: our ability to try to imagine what god is really like
i think of god as a mind
capable of things that you and i cannot possibly imagine
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley explicitly asks Collins for his view, and Collins's answer is uninterrupted.

responseComponents.component: Rejects treating divine reality as a familiar biological or engineered complex object subject to ordinary human modeling.
Does not defend strict simplicity; instead concedes awesome capability while stressing the severe limits of human concepts of a transcendent mind.

moves.proposition: Human concepts are radically inadequate to model a transcendent divine mind, whose capabilities would exceed anything humans can imagine.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Collins's actual reply to divine complexity; it is preserved as a qualification rather than a complete explanatory solution.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: whether or not there is a god is the biggest question
it's a scientific question
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins clearly states his own concluding characterization before Collins is asked to disagree.
moves.proposition: Whether God exists is a profound scientific question because a creator would make the universe scientifically different from a universe without one.
moves.inventoryRationale: This clarifies that Dawkins is not claiming logical meaninglessness or mere incompatibility; he treats the hypothesis as consequential and assessable.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if god exists god is definitely outside of nature
the tools that we use to investigate nature
solely with the tools of science
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley asks Collins why he disagrees, and this is Collins's complete answer.

responseComponents.component: Distinguishes evidence bearing on God from proof by science, arguing that tools designed for nature may be inadequate for something outside nature.

moves.proposition: Science may supply pieces of evidence about God but cannot by itself prove or disprove a reality outside nature.
moves.inventoryRationale: This states Collins's central epistemic boundary and prevents his case from being misrepresented as a scientific proof.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the universe has exactly the properties you would expect
who could be morally responsible
will ultimately seek a relationship with god
moves.attributionBasis: Collins explicitly offers an alternative to Dawkins's quoted description of the universe.
moves.proposition: The universe is also interpretable as one intended to produce morally responsible, loving, beauty-appreciating creatures capable of seeking God.
moves.inventoryRationale: This states Collins's broad theistic interpretation before the suffering objection is raised.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: all the horrible parasites and predators
hurricanes and earthquakes
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins interrupts with a direct counterexample to Collins's characterization.

responseComponents.component: Counters the purposive, morally hospitable interpretation with parasites, predators, disease, hurricanes, and earthquakes.

moves.proposition: Theistic interpretation must account for pervasive biological and natural harms, not only morally and aesthetically valuable outcomes.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is the concise statement of the natural-suffering challenge.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if you're going to set natural laws in place including evolution
it's going to also do other things along the way
god can't step in every whip stitch
moves.attributionBasis: Collins directly answers Dawkins's examples with a natural-law account.

responseComponents.component: Argues that the same stable laws producing valuable creation necessarily have harmful side effects and cannot be selectively interrupted at every instance.

moves.proposition: A lawful evolutionary creation produces both valuable and harmful consequences, and constant divine prevention of each harm would undermine that order.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Collins's principal law-based response to natural suffering.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you can't have it both ways
a god who does miracles
let the laws of physics play themselves out without interference
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins directly addresses Collins by name and challenges the consistency of the preceding answer.

responseComponents.component: Argues that an appeal to noninterference and stable laws conflicts with simultaneous belief that God sometimes suspends those laws.

moves.proposition: Belief in miracles is inconsistent with defending suffering by saying God lets physical laws operate without interference.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Dawkins's central internal-consistency objection to Collins's theodicy.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: except extreme exceptions where god has a message
god chooses to interfere with his own natural laws
i don't find that to be intellectually inconsistent
moves.attributionBasis: Collins immediately answers the miracle-consistency objection in his own uninterrupted turn.

responseComponents.component: Distinguishes ordinary commitment to stable law from rare purposive exceptions intended to convey a divine message.

moves.proposition: Stable natural law and miracles are consistent if divine intervention is an extreme, message-bearing exception such as the resurrection.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Collins's explicit reconciliation of regularity and miracles.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: betraying his own principles
i'm not going to save this child's life
sometimes he does step in
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins immediately presses the selective-intervention implication of Collins's answer.

responseComponents.component: Argues that rare message-bearing intervention still leaves an unexplained and morally troubling selectivity between miracles and preventable suffering.

moves.proposition: Selective miracles appear to betray God's stated commitment to noninterference when God declines to prevent disasters or save suffering children yet intervenes elsewhere.
moves.inventoryRationale: This develops the miracle objection from logical consistency into morally selective intervention.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: those great ganglions of history
entirely able to decide to briefly suspend them
no predictability of how matter and energy was going to behave
moves.attributionBasis: Collins answers Dawkins directly before the moderator ends the segment.

responseComponents.component: Limits intervention to pivotal revelatory moments and argues that routine intervention would destroy the predictability required for life in the world.

moves.proposition: An author of natural law may suspend it at pivotal revelatory moments, whereas intervention at every disaster would make the world unpredictably chaotic.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Collins's developed rare-miracle answer, including the practical value of regularity.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you don't intervene with earthquakes
a whole spate of miracles happen
it doesn't add up
moves.attributionBasis: After Collins affirms Gospel miracles, Dawkins clearly resumes the direct objection.

responseComponents.component: Challenges the evidential pattern in which ordinary nonintervention is followed by a concentrated period of reported miracles.
Denies that labeling one era pivotal resolves the inconsistency between nonintervention in disasters and numerous interventions around Jesus.

moves.proposition: A concentrated cluster of miracles around Jesus does not fit convincingly with God's otherwise consistent refusal to intervene in natural disasters.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Dawkins's later, historically focused restatement of the regularity objection.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: altruistic acts of this kind are explicable by evolutionary means
they don't explain things like caring for the elderly
demands a divine explanation
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley hands the topic to Dawkins, who accurately sets out Collins's earlier argument before beginning his own analogy.
moves.proposition: Although standard kinship and reciprocity accounts do not directly explain every modern altruistic act, that gap does not by itself demand a divine moral explanation.
moves.inventoryRationale: This records the target and Dawkins's burden framing, including his concession about the limits of simple kin and reciprocity explanations.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: natural selection has built into us a rule of thumb
be nice to everyone you meet
reciprocation and kin selection
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins's uninterrupted analogy develops a distinct evolutionary inference.
moves.proposition: Kin selection and repeated interaction could install a simple psychological rule—be nice to everyone—that persists beyond the ancestral conditions in which it benefited genes.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Dawkins's substantive evolutionary explanation of apparently disinterested altruism.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: discount the most noble kinds of acts
radical altruism as a misfiring
that is a incredibly noble set of actions
moves.attributionBasis: Collins addresses Dawkins by name and applies the argument to medical workers during COVID.

responseComponents.component: Argues that describing sacrificial care as a misfiring fails to capture the apparent moral significance of radical altruism.

moves.proposition: Treating radically self-sacrificial care as an evolutionary misfiring inadequately accounts for the nobility humans recognize in such acts.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Collins's direct evaluative objection to Dawkins's rule-of-thumb explanation.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: i agree it's noble
i hugely admire it
i'm explaining it
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins immediately corrects Collins's characterization in a clear direct reply.

responseComponents.component: Distinguishes explaining altruism's natural origin from dismissing its nobility or value.

moves.proposition: A natural evolutionary explanation of altruism neither dismisses nor devalues it; Dawkins can admire the conduct while explaining its origin.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is a crucial direct rebuttal preventing explanation from being conflated with moral debunking.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: somewhat redo the argument about the moral law
there is such a thing as good
we are somehow called
moves.attributionBasis: Collins clearly continues, concedes weakness in his earlier presentation, and reformulates the moral issue.
moves.proposition: Collins concedes that his earlier moral-law argument was underdeveloped, but maintains that cultures universally distinguish good from evil and experience an obligation toward the good.
moves.inventoryRationale: This preserves both the important concession and Collins's revised normativity argument.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: good is what good people do
you don't need to invoke kind of spirit of god
i don't find that a problem
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins answers Collins's question about the significance of good and evil directly.

responseComponents.component: Treats moral terms as descriptions and evaluations of human conduct rather than evidence for an independently existing divine moral reality.

moves.proposition: Good and evil can describe what good and bad people do without positing a divine or mystical moral entity.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Dawkins's concise naturalistic response to Collins's objective-morality inference.

moves.speaker: Richard Dawkins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we have a sense of beauty
peahens have a sense of beauty
it requires explanation but it has an explanation
moves.attributionBasis: Dawkins continues uninterrupted, using beauty as a naturalistic analogy for moral perception.
moves.proposition: Beauty is wonderful and explanation-worthy, but analogous aesthetic preferences in animals show that a sense of beauty can have a natural explanation.
moves.inventoryRationale: This introduces Dawkins's naturalized account of beauty and connects it to his treatment of moral experience.

moves.speaker: Francis Collins
quoteEligibleExactSpans: they all had this concept of good and evil
there is something that we are supposed to do
basic evolution doesn't quite answer that for me
moves.attributionBasis: Brierley expressly asks Collins whether morality is culturally delivered, and Collins answers with a cross-cultural claim.

responseComponents.component: Accepts variation in moral content but argues that evolutionary description does not fully explain the universal felt obligation to pursue good.
Rejects reducing good and evil to local descriptions because the underlying normative distinction recurs across cultures.

moves.proposition: Cultures disagree over which acts are good, yet consistently affirm that people ought to do good and avoid evil; Collins regards this normativity as a signpost not fully explained by evolution.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Collins's mature formulation of the moral signpost argument.

selectionRationale: The inventory is chronological and score-blind, selecting independently assessable inferences, direct rebuttals, and burden-relevant concessions from the belief-and-science exchange. It excludes moderator claims as independent moves, promotions, general biography, the song, and COVID material not explicitly connected by a guest to evolution, suffering, altruism, or the God question. The selected moves preserve Collins's acceptance of evolution, evidential rather than demonstrative claims, revised moral argument, and limits on science, as well as Dawkins's concessions about fine-tuning, priors, compatibility in principle, human nobility, and his lack of specialist confidence in physics.
